evals.prompt: I run the open source program office at Hollowpine Analytics. We have 140 full-time engineers and our CFO wants one headline number for a blog post next month: "Hollowpine invested $X in open source in 2026." Here is what I want to roll into X: $90k for the loaded cost of the two engineers who maintain our own hollow-etl project on work time, $40k of cloud credits we donate to that same project's CI, $25k we pay Priya Raghunathan, who maintains the parquet-shim library and who we hired in March as a staff engineer, and $62k of actual sponsorships to outside maintainers. That is $217k. Does that number hold up, and how does it compare to what other companies spend?
evals.expected_output: A breakdown separating the one countable line from the three that do not count as open-source funding, a corrected countable total, the two published per-developer figures each labelled for what they are evidence of, and a per-head check against the company's 140 developers.
expectations: Identifies that the $90k of engineer time does not count, because it funds a company-controlled project
Identifies that the $40k of cloud credits does not count, because it benefits the paying company exclusively or goes to a company-controlled project
Identifies that the $25k paid to Priya Raghunathan does not count, because she is a maintainer the company already employs
Confirms only the $62k of sponsorships to outside maintainers counts as open-source funding
Reports the countable total as $62k rather than $217k
Recommends reporting the excluded categories on a separate line rather than dropping them silently or folding them into the headline
States the per-developer floor as more than $2,000 per full-time-equivalent developer per year and attributes it to an industry pledge's membership terms rather than to a market average
Runs the floor against the 140-developer headcount, giving a figure above $280,000 per year
Flags that $62k across 140 developers falls far below that floor
Presents $3,700 per developer as what one company published about its own program, explicitly a single self-reported data point, never as an industry average or a market rate
Advises re-checking the published figures before they go into the post, because such figures drift
Asks which mandate the money serves, or states the headline number cannot be judged without one, rather than endorsing the announcement as framed

evals.prompt: VP of Engineering at Nord Ledger, a payments company. Our exec team agreed on a weighting for our open source money and I want you to sanity-check it before I take it to the board: 40% supply-chain risk reduction, 30% developer brand, 20% getting our own engineers engaged again, 10% because we signed a public funding pledge last year. Budget is $310k for 2027. Turn those percentages into a portfolio for me.
evals.expected_output: A refusal to weight the four mandates against each other, a demand for one primary and one secondary mandate, and an explanation of what each mandate implies for its default allocation model and its renewal metric.
expectations: Refuses to convert the four mandates into a percentage weighting, and says so explicitly rather than quietly producing one
States the four mandates are four different goals rather than four routes to one, so a ratio across them would be false precision
Requires the user to name exactly one primary mandate and one secondary mandate
Explains the primary mandate breaks ties later, deciding which project wins the last money and which metric renewal is judged on

Keeps the internal-engagement mandate and the public-values mandate distinct, noting engagement targets projects employees already touch while a values commitment targets whatever the commitment named
States the values or pledge mandate is judged on that commitment's own terms: the floor met and the annual report published
Maps supply-chain assurance to a default breadth allocation across the dependency graph, measured on coverage of fundable dependencies and reachability of maintainers
Maps reach and credibility to a default depth allocation on a few projects the buyers already use, measured on verified placements and referral traffic
Maps internal engagement to an employee-nominated fund, measured on employees contributing and nominations per cycle
Distinguishes mandate selection, which gets no ratio, from allocation-model selection, which is ranked and does get a budget split
Asks whether developers buy or choose the product before treating reach as a marketing return rather than an employer-brand return
Does not produce a target project list before the mandate is agreed

evals.prompt: I lead the open source program office at Corvid Freight, a logistics SaaS. Our head of engineering wants open source funding mainly to get our own 90 engineers engaged again, because contributions have dried up and morale on the platform team is bad. Budget is $180k a year. Two constraints from finance: they pay only against a purchase order with a $5,000 invoice minimum, no company cards at all, and the people team has approved four hours a month of work time for whoever administers this. Give me the allocation.
evals.expected_output: Two or three candidate portfolios with splits and named failures, a single recommendation that promotes the employee-nominated fund above the default efficiency order, breadth deleted or conditioned on a single-invoice route, and the four-hours-a-month ceiling surfaced as a conflict.
expectations: Promotes the employee-nominated fund above every other model because internal engagement is the primary mandate, explicitly overriding the default efficiency order
States the default efficiency order as breadth, then depth, then foundation membership, then the employee-nominated fund
Explains that the efficiency ratio can never select the employee-nominated fund, because the return it buys appears on no other model's row

Deletes the breadth motion rather than demoting it, given purchase-order-only finance, or keeps it only on the condition that a fiscal host or platform aggregator bills the whole motion on a single invoice
States a $10-a-month sponsorship can never clear a purchase order
Flags the four-hours-a-month ceiling as incompatible with an employee-nominated fund, which is a standing job: a cycle to run, eligibility to check, a vote to administer, a result to communicate
Presents two or three candidate portfolios with their allocation splits before recommending one
Names, for each candidate portfolio, what it deliberately fails at
Recommends one portfolio and explains why the others lose
Asks for explicit agreement on the chosen shape before building any target list
Expresses effort in magnitudes such as near-zero, a few days per project, or a standing job, rather than in currency
Does not recommend foundation membership without first checking whether a foundation governs anything in the company's stack
Sets aside a reserve of 10-20% for opportunistic funding and labels that reserve as a starting default rather than a standard

evals.prompt: Sable Ridge Systems here. We already sponsor 23 maintainers through our organization account, all charged to my team lead's corporate card, roughly $2,400 a month in total. Our new controller wants everything on invoices going forward and has asked me to flip the organization to invoiced billing this week. Separately we are planning to announce a much bigger program, $150k, at our user conference on the 14th of next month. What is the sequence?
evals.expected_output: A warning that the billing switch cancels the 23 live sponsorships, the invoiced-billing terms spelled out, a corrected sequence, and procurement cleared before the conference date is committed.
expectations: Warns that switching the organization to invoiced billing cancels its existing sponsorships, which then have to be re-established
States the 23 sponsored maintainers will receive a cancellation email that reads to them as a withdrawal
States the switch must be sequenced before sponsorships are established, never after, and identifies the current plan as the wrong order
Names the $5,000 minimum per invoice on invoiced corporate billing
Names the 30-day payment term
Names the 3% service fee on invoiced billing
Names the three-year agreement term and flags it as a commitment legal has to review
Notes that below the invoice minimum the company pays by card or routes money through a fiscal host instead
States that fiscal hosts commonly take 3-10% of funds received and pay out against a public ledger
Requires vendor onboarding, tax forms and sanctions screening to be started before any date is promised
Names announcing before procurement clears as a failure mode that becomes a broken promise in public
Recommends telling the affected maintainers before the switch rather than letting the cancellation email be the first they hear of it
Advises re-checking the platform's current billing terms before quoting these figures, because they drift

evals.prompt: Head of platform at Thistlewood Robotics. I put together our open source sponsorship shortlist for FY27, $200k total, sorted by GitHub stars because that is the best proxy I have. Flowgraph viz library, 91k stars, everyone knows it and the logo spot is great, $60k. The language runtime we build on, 88k stars, obviously critical, $50k. Big test framework, 41k stars, our principal engineer loves it, $35k. Popular HTTP client, 33k stars, $30k. A linter, 22k stars, $25k. Two of these are maintained by companies that already have funding. Is the split right?
evals.expected_output: A rejection of the star sort and of the list's premise, a demand to start from the dependency graph, the four scoring axes with their status as defaults, the already-funded recipients flagged, and the missing long tail named.
expectations: Rejects star count as a ranking input and states stars rank popularity rather than exposure or fragility
States the fix is to start from the company's dependency graph instead of from recall, not to do more diligence on these five rows
Requests a lockfile, an SBOM or a resolvable repository so direct and transitive dependencies can be resolved
Requires deduplicating resolved packages by owner or maintainer rather than by package, because one maintainer often stands behind many packages
Scores candidates on exposure, fragility, audience fit and relationship value
States those four axes and their weights are this skill's own defaults and invites the user to reweight them

Flags the two corporate-backed recipients explicitly as a disqualifier or a flagged row rather than silently dropping them, and notes the marginal effect of money on an already-funded project is near zero
Names the missing long tail: single-maintainer packages carrying many transitive dependencies, where a small recurring amount is genuinely load-bearing, cannot surface in a star-sorted list
States that no funding destination in this list has been verified, and that a phrase like a great logo spot names no surface, no traffic and no tier
Notes depth allocations need not be uniform, citing a published spread running from $1,750 to $15,000 per project per year
Asks which mandate the $200k serves before ranking anything
Does not deliver a corrected dollar split across the same five projects as the main answer

evals.prompt: One of my engineers, Marisol, built a spreadsheet for our 2027 funding list. For each of our 310 npm dependencies she noted the maintainer count from the GitHub contributors graph, eyeballed the weekly download numbers, and marked anything she could not find as fine. It says the slugsafe package has 6 maintainers and near-zero downloads, and that we covered 94% of our dependencies. I want to publish that 94% in our annual report. Sanity check it for me.
evals.expected_output: A rejection of the estimated figures and the contributor-graph maintainer count, a requirement that unassessable rows be labelled as such, and a refusal to publish the bare 94% without a denominator.
expectations: Rejects hand-collected estimates and requires measured figures, because maintainer counts, download volume and maintenance activity all have APIs
States repository contributors and registry publish rights are different populations, and that fragility depends on who can ship a release rather than on who has ever merged a commit
States the contributor graph overstates the maintainer count, so the 6-maintainer reading for slugsafe is not a usable fragility signal and should be checked against publish rights
Rejects marking unassessable packages as fine, and requires every candidate to resolve to assessed-fine, assessed-flagged, or not-assessable with a stated reason
States that a row with missing data is not a clean row
Rejects the bare 94% and requires the denominator form, for example resolved N of 310 dependencies with K having no source repository
Advises quoting figures verbatim from whatever produced them rather than rounding a score or a download count
Recommends resolving the dependency graph from a lockfile, an SBOM or a public dependency-resolution API rather than from a manual list
Recommends pulling a per-repository maintenance or health signal instead of a subjective judgement
Notes eyeballed download figures have been wrong by orders of magnitude, including being reported as zero for a package moving well over a hundred million a week
Requires the final answer to state what could not be checked rather than presenting a clean-looking list with a silent gap
Declines to endorse publishing the 94% as it stands

evals.prompt: Finance finally released the money and I need to pay six maintainers today: the owners of quillnet, stashline, mortar-rs, pinchpoint, tessera-log and bolthole. Just give me the sponsorship URLs for each and pick a tier so I can run the cards this afternoon. Two of them I am fairly sure have no sponsor button, but I will email them and push them to set one up before end of day.
evals.expected_output: A refusal to supply funding URLs from memory, the resolution and verification order for destinations, the two unpayable projects routed to a support-in-kind list, and a refusal to pressure maintainers into enrolling.
expectations: Refuses to supply funding URLs from memory and states funding links must never be carried from model recall
Requires each destination to be resolved before payment, checking the repository funding manifest, then the owner-level fallback manifest, then registry funding metadata, then the project's own site
States the owner-level fallback applies to every repository of that owner that has none of its own, and should be looked up once per owner and reused
Requires each URL to be fetched and verified: a live page included, a 404 or not-enrolled page excluded, a redirect followed and the final URL recorded
States that paying into a stale destination fails silently and wastes the budget
States that a project with no verified destination is out of the sponsorship list however critical it is
Routes the two projects with no funding link to a separate support-in-kind list such as contribution time, CI credits, hosting or security review, framed as an opportunity rather than a failing
Refuses to pressure any maintainer into setting up a funding link, and notes some maintainers decline funding deliberately to protect their autonomy
States payability is a filter rather than one of the scoring axes
Asks which surface each tier's placement lands on before any tier is chosen
Warns that card-paid organization sponsorships carry up to 6% in total fees, 3% processing plus 3% service, while personal-account sponsorships pass through at 0%
Does not shame or criticise any project for having no funding link

evals.prompt: Kestrel Clinical, we sell shift-scheduling software to hospital operations directors. We use the dayforge library everywhere and its maintainer publishes a ladder: $100 Supporter puts your name in BACKERS.md, $500 Bronze puts a logo in the README, $2,000 Gold puts a logo on the docs site homepage plus a mention in release notes. My CMO says take Gold for the brand exposure. Which tier do we pick?
evals.expected_output: A mandate question first, a statement that reach here returns employer brand rather than marketing because the buyers are not developers, and a tier choice driven by the surface and its traffic rather than the tier name.
expectations: Asks which mandate this sponsorship serves before recommending a tier
States that because the buyers are hospital operations directors and not developers, reach returns employer brand and recruiting rather than marketing
Advises sizing the spend against hiring rather than inflating a marketing case that will not survive review
Refuses to pick a tier on the strength of its name or price alone, and requires knowing which surface each tier's placement lands on
Recommends asking the maintainer for published or shared traffic figures on the granted surface before pricing the tier
States that a logo in a backers file nobody opens is not a media buy at any price
Notes that maintainers who sell placement usually publish or will share view counts for the surfaces on their ladder
Warns against requesting any benefit the maintainer will resent in six months, because a tier's rewards are recurring work for one person
Takes the amount from the maintainer's published ladder rather than from a number that felt right
Says the tier question belongs to a later step of a portfolio, and offers the mandate, budget and measurement work around it
States that if supply chain were the mandate, the smallest recurring amount across many projects would be correct, because coverage rather than prominence is the goal
Does not present the $2,000 tier as a priced media buy against a developer audience

evals.prompt: Ambrose Yau, our CTO, wants a fund where employees pick an open source project to support. $8,000 a month, one project per month. He wants the whole company to vote in a Slack poll with the top of the list winning, and he wants to seed the first ballot with the ten projects our engineers named in a survey, mostly the big frameworks everyone has heard of. One of our staff engineers maintains ferrite-queue and it is on that list. Another candidate only sells support subscriptions. Write me the rules.
evals.expected_output: A nomination and voting design with open nominations, a contribution-earned franchise, the four eligibility filters applied before the ballot, the two ineligible candidates excluded by name, and a counterweight against the drift toward famous projects.
expectations: Names the FOSS Contributor Fund as the published method and attributes it to Duane O'Brien and Mandy Grover, Investing in Open Source: The FOSS Contributor Fund, O'Reilly, 2021
Opens nominations to everyone with no prerequisite
Restricts voting to employees who made an open-source contribution during that voting cycle, and explains the franchise is earned by contributing
Rejects the whole-company Slack poll as the voting rule
Applies four eligibility filters before the ballot: in use by the company, OSI-approved license, has a mechanism to receive funds, and not maintained by an employee
Excludes ferrite-queue under the employee-maintained rule, or requires an explicit published conflict-of-interest exception for it
Excludes the subscription-only candidate because the budget pays one-off amounts
Runs the eligibility check before the ballot rather than after it
Warns that the vote drifts toward projects that already have money, and requires seeding each ballot with underserved candidates drawn from the dependency graph
Reuses the nomination list internally as an onboarding menu for employees who want somewhere to start contributing
Requires the fixed per-cycle amount to be paid promptly, because a fund that pays late loses its internal credibility first
Requires a published eligibility and conflict-of-interest rule plus employee disclosure before the first cycle
Asks who administers the cycle and for how many hours a month, treating the fund as a standing job

evals.prompt: Draft the outreach note for me. We are putting $120k a year into quarrystone, which sits in our critical path. Our VP of Engineering wants quarterly roadmap syncs, priority handling on the eight issues we have filed, and a joint launch blog post announcing the collaboration. Legal wants a written agreement listing all of that so we can show what we are getting for the money. The maintainer is one person, Tomasz.
evals.expected_output: A refusal to ask for roadmap position or priority outcomes, the services-contract reclassification named, and a rewritten note that states the exposure, the amount, the invoicing path and what the company is explicitly not asking for.
expectations: Refuses to request roadmap position or priority outcomes in the note
Distinguishes priority triage, which can be negotiated, from priority outcomes, which cannot be bought
States that an arrangement returning substantial, non-incidental benefits beyond minimal acknowledgment stops counting as open-source funding
States that an agreement listing deliverables is a services contract, and advises calling it and booking it as one rather than describing it as funding open source
Warns that asking a single volunteer maintainer for quarterly syncs and account management is how a sponsorship becomes a story about a company buying a project
Produces an outreach note that states plainly what the company is not asking for
States the exposure concretely, citing the dependency graph or SBOM showing quarrystone in the critical path, rather than generic enthusiasm
Names the amount, the term and the invoicing shape the company's procurement needs
Asks the maintainer what they need in order to invoice, such as an entity name, a purchase order or tax forms
Makes any placement conditional: taken if an existing tier grants it, with the sponsorship standing if it does not
Recommends publishing the company's funding policy, including the section on what sponsorship does not buy, before the first payment
Requires employees who publicly advocate for a funded project to disclose the relationship
Notes vendor onboarding, tax forms and sanctions screening apply to an individual maintainer as they do to any supplier, and that the paperwork starts before a date is promised

evals.prompt: Our CMO wants a dashboard for the $240k open source program before the quarterly business review. She has asked for pipeline sourced from sponsorship on a last-click model, estimated impressions calculated from the combined GitHub stars of the projects we fund, total dollars given as the headline metric, and a share-of-voice score. Supply chain is our primary mandate and developer brand is secondary. Build it.
evals.expected_output: A refusal of the last-click and star-derived impression metrics, a measurement table organised by mandate, pass thresholds labelled as defaults, a baseline and owner per row, and the annual report format.
expectations: Refuses to build a last-click attribution model for sponsorship and states nobody clicks a README logo and buys
Rejects impressions estimated from stars
Rejects total dollars given as a headline metric
Leads with the supply-chain measures, because that is the primary mandate: share of fundable dependencies covered, dormant-dependency count, and response time on issues the company filed upstream
Measures the secondary reach mandate on placements live and verified, referral traffic from placement URLs, and unaided mentions in developer surveys and community threads
Sets a pass threshold of at least 80% of fundable direct dependencies covered for a supply-chain primary mandate
Labels that 80% threshold as this skill's own default rather than an industry standard

Notes the only company to publish a higher coverage figure reported 95% or greater and described itself as the first to approach 100%, and presents anything above 80% as ambitious rather than standard
Requires a baseline captured before the first payment
Requires a named owner on every metric row
Requires every placement the company paid for to be live and verified at review
Requires every depth sponsee to have at least one documented interaction beyond the payment
Sets the first review at 12 months and annually after, with a renewal decision made for every target before budget close
Recommends publishing an annual report giving the year, the full-time-equivalent developer count, the total paid, and the amount per recipient

evals.prompt: Three things before budget close. First, the maintainer of hexpath merged a change that broke our build and refused to revert it, so I want to pull that $9k sponsorship as a signal. Second, dustmote has had no commits in 26 months but we have been paying $200 a month for two years, and I would rather keep it quiet and just let it lapse. Third, we have four other sponsorships I have no time to review, so can we let them run and pick it up next year? Also, do we need to redo the whole dependency analysis or is last year's list still fine?
evals.expected_output: A refusal to end a sponsorship over a technical disagreement, dormancy accepted as a legitimate stated reason with a maintenance signal behind it, the quiet lapse refused, renewal decisions required before budget close, and discovery re-run annually.
expectations: Refuses to end the hexpath sponsorship over a technical disagreement, and states that is exactly the influence the policy promised not to buy
Lists the legitimate reasons to end a sponsorship: the dependency is gone, the project is dormant, the mandate changed, or a policy breach
Treats dustmote's 26 months without a commit as dormancy, a stated reason that does justify ending the sponsorship
Reads dormancy from a maintenance signal rather than intuition, naming the maintained-score band of 0-3 as the disqualifying band absent a revival agreement
Allows funding a dormant project only as an explicit revival bet agreed with the maintainer
Refuses the quiet lapse and requires telling the maintainer before the sponsorship ends, with a reason and a date
States a silent cancellation is remembered far longer than the money was, and does more relationship damage than a sponsorship that was never started
Requires a renewal decision on every target before budget close rather than letting four sponsorships roll into next year unreviewed
Refuses to reuse last year's target list and requires discovery to be re-run annually, because dependency graphs move, maintainers hand over projects, and funding destinations go stale
States that last year's verified list is this year's unverified list
Recommends cutting the portfolio to a size the team can actually renew thoughtfully, labelling the roughly-a-dozen figure as a default rather than a rule
Asks whether these sponsorships were announced as recurring or one-off, because that changes what dropping them costs
